# Artificial light reorients nocturnal dung beetles

A ball-rolling dung beetle has to get away from the dung pile before
competitors take its ball. Holding a steady bearing helps it roll away
along a straight path. Beetles can use the same sky cues to hold
different bearings, so individuals leaving in different directions
can each be well oriented. Nocturnal species can use the moon and its
polarization pattern or, on moonless nights, the starry sky. Artificial
light can obscure faint sky cues, and a bright local lamp can provide
a bearing that many beetles follow.

We revisit a field experiment by
[Foster et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2021.06.038)
with nocturnal dung beetles (*Escarabaeus satyrus*) in South Africa.
The same beetles rolled their balls under natural nighttime illumination
and with a floodlight to the southwest. If the lamp acts as a beacon,
we expect bearings to shift toward it and different beetles to head
in more similar directions. A separate question is whether the lamp
changes how reliably each beetle repeats its own bearing.

## Compare the lighting conditions

Gray marks the natural-light control (floodlight off), and gold marks
the floodlight treatment. The lamp's position defines the same southwest
reference bearing in both conditions. That lets us ask how often beetles
would exit toward that part of the arena even with the lamp off.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-05"


save_figure <- function(plot, name, width = 8, height = 4) {
  ggsave(file.path(FIG_DIR, paste0(name, ".pdf")), plot,
         width = width, height = height)
  show_figure(plot, name, width, height)
}

# Same published source files as the Python loaders; keep their local
# checkout under the repository root, reachable from notebooks_r/ too.
# An existing checkout can be supplied through UNWRAP_DATA_ROOT.
data_root <- Sys.getenv("UNWRAP_DATA_ROOT",
                        unset = file.path(repo_root, "unwrap-data"))
ensure_data <- function(subdir) {
  target <- file.path(data_root, subdir)
  if (!dir.exists(target)) {
    if (!dir.exists(data_root)) {
      status <- system2("git", c("clone", "--depth", "1",
        "--filter=blob:none", "--sparse",
        "https://github.com/jgraving/unwrap-data.git", shQuote(data_root)))
      if (status != 0L) stop("Could not fetch the published study data.")
    }
    # Sparse checkout downloads only this study; later notebooks may add
    # their own subdirectory to the same checkout without replacing it.
    status <- system2("git", c("-C", shQuote(data_root),
                              "sparse-checkout", "add", subdir))
    if (status != 0L) stop("Could not materialize the study subdirectory.")
  }
  stopifnot(dir.exists(target))
  target
}

```

## Compare repeated exits from the arena

Each beetle starts with its ball at the center of a circular arena
one meter across. After each exit it is returned to the center for
another trial. The response is the bearing from the center to the
point where the beetle reaches the boundary. The design called for ten
exits in each lighting condition for each of ten beetles. Four
floodlight-on bearings are missing, leaving 100 control and 96
treatment bearings.

The two conditions are paired within beetle. Repeated exits reveal how
steadily each beetle follows its own bearing, and comparing conditions
within the same beetle separates its response to the lamp from
persistent differences in bearing among beetles.

### Read the observed bearings

Each panel shows one beetle. The angle of a point gives the exit bearing,
and its distance from the center gives the trial number. The solid and
dashed spokes mark the circular mean and median. The shaded wedge shows
one circular standard deviation to either side of the mean. Its width
describes how spread out the exits were.

Angles wrap around, so exits at 355° and 5° are both close to north and
have a circular mean of 0°. To find that mean, treat each bearing as an
arrow of length one and take the direction of the average arrow. In the
plots, beetle 1 shifts from near north toward the southwest, whereas
beetle 4 already tended toward the southwest with the lamp off. The
different starting bearings and different shifts motivate a model with
both a baseline and a treatment effect for each beetle.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-07"

                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)

data <- data.frame(Light = as.integer(grepl("ON", raw$Experiment, fixed = TRUE)),
  Individual = raw$Beetle, Trial = raw$Trial,
  HeadingRadians = mod_circular(heading * pi / 180))
data <- data[complete.cases(data), ]
data$Individual <- factor(data$Individual)
condition_labels <- c("light OFF", "light ON")
condition_colors <- c("light OFF" = "#9e9e9e", "light ON" = "#f4a300")
# Hex values are the Python notebook's ON/OFF pair, shared by every
# condition-colored figure in this study.
data$condition <- factor(data$Light, levels = 0:1, labels = condition_labels)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(data$HeadingRadians)), all(abs(data$HeadingRadians) <= pi))
head(data)

```

## Model direction and consistency together

For beetle $i$ in lighting condition $x$, a von Mises distribution
describes the distribution of repeated exit bearings. Its mean direction
$\mu_i(x)$ gives the beetle's preferred bearing, and its concentration
$\kappa_i(x)$ describes how consistently the beetle returns to it.
When $\kappa=0$, all bearings are equally likely. Larger $\kappa$ puts
more probability close to $\mu$.

### Give each beetle a baseline and a response to the light

Let $x=0$ denote light off and $x=1$ light on. The model uses a separate
predictor for direction and for concentration.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i(x) &= \operatorname{wrap}\bigl(\beta_0+\beta_1 x+b_{0,i}+b_{1,i}x\bigr),\\
\kappa_i(x) &= \operatorname{softplus}\bigl(\alpha_0+\alpha_1 x+a_{0,i}+a_{1,i}x\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

The population terms $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ give the baseline direction
and the angular shift with the lamp on. The offsets $b_{0,i}$ and
$b_{1,i}$ let beetle $i$ have its own starting bearing and its own
response. Wrapping the sum treats bearings a full turn apart as the
same direction. The concentration terms $\alpha$ and $a$ play the
same baseline and treatment roles on a different scale. Softplus maps
their sum to a positive concentration. To interpret a change in
$\kappa$, compare the transformed concentrations with the lamp on and
off.

### Share information across beetles

The individual offsets are centered around zero. Their spread
determines how much individual estimates are pulled toward the
population baseline and treatment effect. With roughly ten exits per
beetle per condition, this partial pooling helps distinguish persistent
individual differences from trial-to-trial variation. A beetle with
imprecise estimates can borrow information from the others.

The prior gives nearly equal weight to all population baseline
directions and favors smaller angular shifts. On the concentration
scale it puts the typical baseline near $\kappa=5$. The prior for the
treatment coefficient is centered at zero before the softplus
transformation, allowing either an increase or a decrease.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-10"
# Preserve independent circular intercept and slope deviations. brms's
# ordinary (1 + Light | Individual) mu term would impose Gaussian effects.
# Following the Rmd, represent them as nonlinear coefficient vectors.
form_vonmises <- bf(HeadingRadians ~ mu,
  nlf(mu ~ beta0 + bias0 + Light * bias1),
  beta0 ~ 1 + Light,
  bias0 ~ 0 + Individual,
  bias1 ~ 0 + Individual,
  kappa ~ 0 + Intercept + Light + (1 + Light || Individual),
  family = unwrap_von_mises)

# One LogNormal(log(30), 0.5) hyperprior for each direction-effect vector,
# as in Python. Direct positive parameters need no softplus Jacobian.
stan_direction_priors <- stanvar(scode = "
  real<lower=0> kmu_intercept;
  real<lower=0> kmu_slope;
", block = "parameters") + stanvar(scode = "
  real unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(vector y, real mu, real kappa) {
    real lp = 0;
    for (i in 1:num_elements(y)) {
      lp += unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(y[i] | mu, kappa);
    }
    return lp;
  }
", block = "functions")
prior_vonmises <- (
  # The direction coefficients are unconstrained reals, matching the
  # Python twin's circ_mod parameterization: its von Mises coefficient
  # priors are periodic over the real line and carry no +-pi bounds.
  # Each coefficient's prior is its von Mises log density, added as an
  # explicit target term (the weak-kappa 1e-6 intercept term is
  # effectively flat over any 2*pi window; a uniform prior is NOT used:
  # bounded uniform boxes pin NUTS chains against the +-pi walls). The
  # generated Stan for this prior set is free of brms's default Gaussian
  # on the direction coefficients (verified at build time in the fit
  # cell).
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(b_beta0[1] | 0, 1e-6)", check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(b_beta0[2] | 0, 2)", check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(b_bias0 | 0, kmu_intercept)",
            check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(b_bias1 | 0, kmu_slope)",
            check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += lognormal_lpdf(kmu_intercept | log(30), 0.5)",
            check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += lognormal_lpdf(kmu_slope | log(30), 0.5)",
            check = FALSE) +
  prior("normal(log(exp(5) - 1), 1)", class = "b", dpar = "kappa",
        coef = "Intercept") +
  prior("normal(0, 1)", class = "b", dpar = "kappa",
        coef = "Light") +
  prior("normal(0, 1)", class = "sd", dpar = "kappa")
)
# EQUIVALENCE NOTE: || removes brms's default intercept/slope correlation;
# the Python priors are separate independent effects, with no LKJ term.
# Gaussian kappa effects use brms's non-centered parameterization and
# positive sd bounds turn normal(0, 1) into HalfNormal(1).
# The nonlinear mu vectors retain centered von Mises effects, not normal
# random effects. Verify their generated names/bounds/priors when baking.
prior_vonmises
```

## Estimate the posterior

Bayesian inference combines the priors with the likelihood of the
observed exit bearings. Each posterior draw gives one plausible set of
population and individual effects. Within that draw we can calculate
both lighting conditions, take their difference, and then summarize the
differences across draws. This keeps the uncertainty shared by the
two conditions in the treatment contrast.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-12"
# Inspect the generated Stan before sampling: every direction
# coefficient must be an UNCONSTRAINED real (the Python circ_mod
# geometry - periodic von Mises priors, no +-pi bounds) and each
# coefficient's von Mises prior must appear as a target term.
stan_code <- make_stancode(form_vonmises, data = data,
  prior = prior_vonmises,
  stanvars = stan_unwrap_fun + modulo_circular_fun + stan_direction_priors)
stopifnot(grepl("vector[K_beta0] b_beta0;", stan_code, fixed = TRUE),
          grepl("vector[K_bias0] b_bias0;", stan_code, fixed = TRUE),
          grepl("vector[K_bias1] b_bias1;", stan_code, fixed = TRUE),
          !grepl("uniform_lpdf", stan_code, fixed = TRUE),
          grepl("kmu_intercept", stan_code, fixed = TRUE),
          grepl("unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf", stan_code, fixed = TRUE))

# NUTS on the unbounded angular coefficients: the priors and the
# likelihood depend on them only modulo 2*pi, so the total posterior is
# a countable family of 2*pi-equivalent classes (the per-individual
# heading sums straddle the angular seam), separated by high posterior
# barriers. Chains exploring different classes fail sine R-hat/ESS even
# though every chain is individually converged. Seed all chains in one
# class from the data: intercept anchor = base-condition circular mean,
# slope anchor = wrapped circular mean difference, per-individual
# deviation anchors = wrapped condition-mean differences, jitter too
# small to cross any seam. Initialization changes only the sampler path,
# never the posterior.
g_off_ind <- as.numeric(tapply(data$HeadingRadians[data$Light == 0],
  data$Individual[data$Light == 0], circ_mean))
g_on_ind <- as.numeric(tapply(data$HeadingRadians[data$Light == 1],
  data$Individual[data$Light == 1], circ_mean))
mu_anchor <- as.numeric(circ_mean(data$HeadingRadians[data$Light == 0]))
ls_anchor <- as.numeric(mod_circular(
  circ_mean(data$HeadingRadians[data$Light == 1]) -
  circ_mean(data$HeadingRadians[data$Light == 0])))
stopifnot(length(g_off_ind) == length(levels(data$Individual)),
  length(g_on_ind) == length(levels(data$Individual)),
  abs(mu_anchor) < pi - 0.2, abs(ls_anchor) < pi - 0.5)
mk_init <- function(anchor_seed) {
  set.seed(anchor_seed)
  j <- function(n) runif(n, -0.08, 0.08)
  list(b_beta0 = as.numeric(c(mu_anchor + j(1), ls_anchor + j(1))),
    b_bias0 = as.numeric(mod_circular(g_off_ind - mu_anchor) + j(length(g_off_ind))),
    b_bias1 = as.numeric(mod_circular(g_on_ind - mu_anchor - ls_anchor) + j(length(g_on_ind))),
    kmu_intercept = 30, kmu_slope = 30)
}
fit <- unwrap_load_fit_cache("beetles_fit_v2", SEED, ITER, WARMUP)
if (is.null(fit)) {
  fit <- brm(form_vonmises, data = data,
    stanvars = stan_unwrap_fun + modulo_circular_fun + stan_direction_priors,
    prior = prior_vonmises, backend = "cmdstanr",
    chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP, cores = CHAINS,
    seed = SEED,
    init = lapply(seq_len(CHAINS), function(k) mk_init(SEED + k)),
    control = list(adapt_delta = ADAPT_DELTA))
  unwrap_save_fit_cache("beetles_fit_v2", fit, SEED, ITER, WARMUP)
}
```

## Check the posterior estimates

Before interpreting the treatment effects, check whether the sampling
chains explore the same range of plausible values. $\hat R$ near 1
indicates agreement between chains, and effective sample size estimates
how many independent draws would provide comparable precision.
Divergent transitions can indicate that the chains had difficulty
exploring parts of the posterior. Read angular estimates on the circle,
where an interval can cross the wrap point and its upper endpoint may
appear numerically smaller than its lower endpoint.

The saved fit has no entries in the flagged $\hat R$ and bulk effective
sample size table. The cached fit has no recorded divergence count.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-14"


available <- posterior::variables(posterior::as_draws_array(fit))
circular_parameters <- available[grepl("^b_(beta0|bias0|bias1)_", available)]
summary_frame <- diagnose_fit(fit, circular_parameters)
summary_frame

```

## Interpret the response to artificial light

### Which way did beetles reorient?

The curves on the polar plot show the posterior distribution of the
population mean direction $\mu$ in each condition. The points on the
outer ring show the observed mean bearing of each beetle. With the
light on, the gold curve moves toward the marked southwest sector and
the individual means bunch near it. The estimated population shift is
about 72° on average. The width of each curve describes uncertainty
about the population mean direction. To see how tightly an individual
beetle repeated its exits, look at the concentration panel.

### How much did consistency and agreement change?

- **Within-individual concentration** asks how tightly a typical
  beetle's exits cluster around its own preferred bearing. The panel
  expresses the population-level $\kappa$ as the expected mean
  resultant length $R(\kappa)=I_1(\kappa)/I_0(\kappa)$. On this
  scale, values near zero indicate very dispersed bearings and values
  near one indicate tightly clustered bearings. The fitted values are
  high in both conditions, rising modestly from about 0.89 to 0.92.
- **Between-individual concentration** asks how closely the ten
  beetles' fitted preferred bearings agree. Give each beetle one unit
  arrow pointing along its fitted mean and take the length of their
  average. Arrows pointing in different directions cancel, while
  similar directions produce a long resultant. This measure rises
  from roughly 0.3 to 0.9 with the light on. Beetles can be consistent
  even when their preferred directions are far apart, as in the control.

### How likely was an exit near the floodlight?

For each posterior draw we calculate how much of the von Mises
distribution falls within 45° of the lamp on either side. The
calculation uses the population direction and concentration, which
describe a beetle whose individual offsets are zero. This probability
combines direction and concentration. Tighter exits increase the
probability when they cluster near the lamp and can decrease it when
they cluster elsewhere.

The sector occupies $90^\circ/360^\circ=25\%$ of the circle, so the
dashed line shows the prediction if all bearings were equally likely.
The fitted probability rises from roughly 10% with the lamp off to
70% with it on. The final panel subtracts off from on within each
draw, giving an estimated increase of about 60 percentage points.
The points and bars are posterior means and 89% highest-density
intervals. The change is clearly positive in the figure, with
substantial uncertainty about its size.

The additional density plot shows the full posterior for the change.
Values to the right of the zero line represent an increase in the
probability of exiting toward the lamp.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-18"
# Draw x individual-condition matrices from the fitted model; the
# per-draw direction and concentration matrices feed the summary
# panels, the alignment statistic and the PPC cells below (twin of
# the Python posthoc computation).
posterior <- posterior_directions(fit, data, condition_labels)
ids <- posterior$ids
prediction_data <- posterior$prediction_data
mu <- posterior$mu
kappa <- posterior$kappa
J <- posterior$J
pre <- posterior$pre
post <- posterior$post
group_alignment <- posterior$group_alignment
individual_summary <- posterior$individual_summary
p_individual <- individual_plot(individual_summary, condition_colors)
save_figure(p_individual, "individual_posteriors", 10, 6)
```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-19"
fixed <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit))
population_mu <- cbind(mod_circular(fixed$b_beta0_Intercept),
  mod_circular(fixed$b_beta0_Intercept + fixed$b_beta0_Light))
theta <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = 361)
mu_kde <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(c) {
  data.frame(theta = theta %% (2 * pi),
    density = vapply(theta, function(t) mean(exp(vm_logpdf(t, population_mu[, c], 80))), numeric(1)),
    condition = condition_labels[c])
}))
# Polar population-mu KDE following the Python twin (beetles_plots.py,
# plot_polar_mu_kde): the radius is 0.5 + 0.5 * kde/max_kde, so the
# density-zero ring sits at radius 0.5 and the shared peak at 1.0. The
# outer reference ring at radius 1.11 carries each beetle's per-condition
# circular mean; the floodlight sector at -135 +/- 45 degrees is a black
# arc with end-and-centre ticks. The twin carries no tick labels here.
max_kde_mu <- max(mu_kde$density)
ring_base <- 0.5
mu_kde$base <- ring_base
mu_kde$r <- ring_base + 0.5 * mu_kde$density / max_kde_mu
r_pts <- ring_base + 0.5 * 1.22
# The marked arc is the +/-45-degree floodlight sector, centered at -135.
flood_dir <- -3 * pi / 4
r_on_max <- max(mu_kde$r[mu_kde$condition == condition_labels[2]])
r_mark <- r_on_max + 0.4 * (r_pts - r_on_max)
cap <- 0.03 * r_pts
flood_arc <- data.frame(theta = seq(flood_dir - pi / 4, flood_dir + pi / 4,
  length.out = 100L) %% (2 * pi), r = r_mark)
flood_ticks <- data.frame(theta = c(flood_dir - pi / 4, flood_dir,
  flood_dir + pi / 4) %% (2 * pi), lo = r_mark - cap, hi = r_mark + cap)
ind_means <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(data, list(data$Individual,
  data$condition), drop = TRUE), function(g) data.frame(
    theta = circ_mean(g$HeadingRadians) %% (2 * pi),
    condition = g$condition[1])))
ind_means$r <- r_pts
p_mu <- polar_mu_kde_plot(mu_kde, theta, r_pts, flood_arc, flood_ticks,
  ind_means, condition_colors)
save_figure(p_mu, "treat_polar_mu_kde_clean", 3.0, 3.0)

# Python's main treatment figure uses the fixed-effect (zero individual
# deviation) concentration and predictive density, not an average over
# the observed individuals or a marginal prediction for a new individual.
population_kappa <- cbind(softplus(fixed$b_kappa_Intercept),
  softplus(fixed$b_kappa_Intercept + fixed$b_kappa_Light))
FLOOD_DIR <- -135 * pi / 180
arc <- seq(FLOOD_DIR - pi / 4, FLOOD_DIR + pi / 4, length.out = 181)
delta <- diff(arc)[1]
flood_mass <- matrix(0, nrow = nrow(population_mu), ncol = 2)
for (j in 1:2) {
  weights <- c(0.5, rep(1, length(arc) - 2), 0.5)
  for (a in seq_along(arc)) {
    flood_mass[, j] <- flood_mass[, j] + weights[a] * delta *
      exp(vm_logpdf(arc[a], population_mu[, j], population_kappa[, j]))
  }
}
within_R <- A1_safe(population_kappa)
mass <- flood_mass
treatment_statistics <- list("within-individual R(kappa)" = within_R,
  "between-individual alignment" = group_alignment,
  "probability within 45 degrees of floodlight" = mass)
# Python-twin treatment figure: one row of four 8 x 3 panels --
# within-individual concentration, between-individual concentration,
# floodlight attraction (dashed Uniform reference at the 25% sector
# mass) and the ON-minus-Off change in that mass. Vertical error bars
# per condition (Off grey / On gold), mean marker + 89% HDI with caps,
# value on a 0-1 y axis.
p_concentration <- treatment_hdi_row(population_kappa, group_alignment,
  flood_mass, condition_colors)
save_figure(p_concentration, "treat_concentration_plus_floodlight", 8, 3)
mass_delta <- data.frame(delta = mass[, 2] - mass[, 1])
p_mass_delta <- mass_delta_plot(mass_delta)
save_figure(p_mass_delta, "floodlight_mass_change", 6, 3)

```

## Estimate the change in agreement among beetles

The figure reports agreement on the 0-to-1 resultant length scale.
Here we express the same pattern as a von Mises concentration
$\kappa_\mu$. We find the concentration that would give the same
length of the average arrow for the fitted preferred bearings, by
inverting $R(\kappa)$. Each beetle contributes one bearing. This gives
a separate summary of clustering among the ten fitted means.

### Compare the estimated mean directions

First summarize each beetle by its posterior mean direction in each
condition. These point estimates give $\kappa_\mu$ of about 0.6 with
the light off and 5.3 with it on.

### Carry uncertainty into the contrast

Repeat the calculation separately for each posterior draw. Reconstruct
all ten beetles' mean directions with the light off and on, convert
each set's resultant length to $\kappa_\mu$, and subtract off from on
within the draw. This carries uncertainty about the fitted bearings
through to uncertainty in the change. It also keeps the calculation at
the level of the beetles' preferred bearings even when their exits
vary from trial to trial.

The posterior mean increase in $\kappa_\mu$ is about 4.6, with a 95%
highest-density interval of roughly 2.7 to 7. Stronger agreement among
the beetles is consistent with many individuals using the same local
beacon. That convergence could make it harder for beetles to disperse
in different directions away from the dung pile. The arena response
measures exit bearings, so the contrast speaks directly to their
orientation in this setting.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-21"
individual_point <- apply(mu, 2, circ_mean)
kappamu_point <- c(OFF = inverse_A1(resultant(individual_point[pre])),
                    ON = inverse_A1(resultant(individual_point[post])))
kappamu_point

```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-22"
kappamu <- apply(group_alignment, 2, function(r) vapply(r, inverse_A1, numeric(1)))
kappamu <- cbind(kappa_mu_OFF = kappamu[, 1], kappa_mu_ON = kappamu[, 2],
                  kappa_mu_delta = kappamu[, 2] - kappamu[, 1])
stopifnot(all(is.finite(kappamu)))
kappamu_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(kappamu), function(p) {
  data.frame(parameter = p, as.list(interval_row(kappamu[, p])))
}))
kappamu_summary

```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-23"
mean(kappamu[, "kappa_mu_delta"] > 0)

```

## Check the circular summaries against the observations

Do the main features inferred by the model also show up when we summarize
the raw bearings? The open markers are bootstrap estimates from repeated
resamples of the observed exits. For the group summaries we resample
whole beetles, keeping their two lighting conditions paired, and then
resample trials within each selected beetle and condition. Each selected
beetle contributes one mean bearing to the group summary. For the
individual panels we resample trials within each beetle and condition.

The filled markers summarize the fitted posterior. The upper left
panel compares the circular average of the resampled beetle means
with the population direction estimated by the model. The upper
right panel compares agreement among beetles. In the
lower panels, compare each beetle's mean direction and its within-beetle
resultant length. The 95% intervals describe uncertainty from resampling
for the open markers and uncertainty under the fitted model for the
filled markers. Both approaches show a tighter grouping of individual
bearings with the lamp on. With the lamp off, the group direction is
less precisely estimated, consistent with beetles heading in more
varied directions. Differences between the markers help locate where
the model and the raw-data summaries differ.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-25"
# Python's supplemental PPC compares data bootstraps with fitted response
# parameters (not with a new stochastic dataset). Reproduce that check,
# then add a conventional replicated-data check below.
B_GROUP <- if (quick_run) 200L else 2000L
B_INDIV <- if (quick_run) 150L else 1500L
ys <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(prediction_data)), function(j) {
  data$HeadingRadians[as.character(data$Individual) ==
    as.character(prediction_data$Individual[j]) &
    data$Light == prediction_data$Light[j]]
})
stopifnot(all(lengths(ys) > 0L))
# The data-bootstrap vs posterior comparison (Python's supplemental
# PPC) runs in the sourced posthoc script; the seed stays here.
set.seed(SEED + 10L)
ppc_boot <- ppc_bootstrap_stats(fit, prediction_data, ys, J,
  B_GROUP, B_INDIV, condition_labels, group_alignment)
# Python-twin supplemental PPC (beetle_posterior_predictive_check):
# group mean direction (a) and group alignment (b) by condition on top,
# per-individual mean direction (c = OFF, d = ON) and per-individual
# concentration (e = OFF, f = ON) below. Bootstrap = open marker,
# posterior = filled; light OFF grey, light ON gold; circular intervals
# wrapped to 0-360 degrees with minimal-arc error widths.
ppc_twin <- ppc_twin_plot(J, ids, individual_summary,
  ppc_boot$boot_individual, ppc_boot$boot_group_mu, ppc_boot$boot_group_R,
  ppc_boot$population_mu, group_alignment, condition_labels, condition_colors)
save_figure(ppc_twin, "beetle_posterior_predictive_check", 8.8,
  max(3.4, 0.28 * J + 2.2))

```

### Check concentration in replicated exits

Would the fitted model generate sets of exits as tightly clustered as
those we observed? For each sampled posterior draw, use each beetle's
fitted direction and concentration to simulate the same number of exits
recorded in that condition. Compute the sample resultant length
for each simulated set, just as for the observed exits. The replicated
values reflect both uncertainty in the fitted parameters and the
trial-to-trial variation expected in a new set of exits.

The open circles show observed resultant lengths. The filled circles
and bars show the means and 95% highest-density intervals of the
replicated lengths. Look for a pattern of observed points above or
below the intervals. The saved figure shows no consistent mismatch
across beetles or conditions in this measure of within-beetle spread.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "beetles-27"
# Same observed sample sizes, each animal's own conditional likelihood.
# Limit simulation draws only; MCMC fitting still uses the budgets above.
set.seed(SEED + 20L)
draw_ids <- sample.int(nrow(mu), min(nrow(mu), if (quick_run) 100L else 400L))
rep_stats <- replicated_stats(mu, kappa, ys, draw_ids, prediction_data)
p_replicates <- replicated_r_plot(rep_stats, condition_colors)
save_figure(p_replicates, "ppc_replicated", 10, 4)

```
